subject: geography
title: Fieldwork Adventure: Data Presentation
welcome_lead: Numbers tell stories — but only if you pick the right graph. Time to choose wisely.
meta_desc: GCSE Geography data presentation — scatter, bar, line, pie, choropleth, isoline maps.
final_note: You learned the main graph and map types and when to use each.

concepts.def: Shows change over time — continuous data
Shows proportions of a whole — percentages
Bar chart drawn on a map at sample location

walkthroughs.body_html:
Bar chart: comparing categories (e.g. pedestrians in 5 streets).

Line graph: change over time (river discharge through the day).

Scatter graph: relationship (river depth vs distance downstream).

Pie chart: parts of a whole (% by land use).

Choropleth: shaded map — e.g. average house price by ward. Darker = higher. Easy to read, hides within-area variation.

Isoline map: lines join equal values (like contour lines or pressure isobars).

Dot map: a dot for each unit (e.g. 1 dot = 100 people).

Located bar/pie: place chart at each sample site on a base map.

When describing a graph, use the acronym TEA:

Trend (overall pattern).
Evidence (use figures).
Anomalies (outliers).

For a scatter: state direction (positive/negative), strength (strong/weak), and quote any outliers with their value.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data in geography fieldwork?
options: Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.
Primary data is more important and secondary data is less reliable.
Primary data is collected in primary schools and secondary data in secondary schools.
Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher (surveys, measurements, observations); secondary data already exists and is found in sources (census data, maps, published reports).

mcqs.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative data?
options: Quantitative data is numerical and measurable (traffic counts, river width); qualitative data is descriptive and non-numerical (interview quotes, photo descriptions, field sketches).
Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.
Quantitative data is always more scientific and reliable than qualitative.
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between random, stratified and systematic sampling?
options: Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.
All three sampling methods produce the same results.

Random: every member has equal chance of selection. Systematic: pick every nth item. Stratified: divide the population into groups and sample proportionally from each — ensures subgroup representation.
Primary data is collected in primary schools and secondary data in secondary schools.
